title: Light-addressed foil cells: optical row strobes replace wordline drivers
idea: Give each printed cell an access TFT whose gate is charged by a small printed photodiode, and address rows by flashing a micro-LED line array beneath the transparent foil, so no metal wordline or high-voltage driver exists.
why: Wordline CV^2 at ~3 V (fact 10) and driver periphery (fact 7) vanish; a 2 fC gate charge needs ~12,500 photons, ~4 fJ per cell; speculative because printed photodiodes must respond within ~10 ns.

title: Sandwich bonding: sense wafer below, wordline-driver wafer above array
idea: Fabricate the cell array on a wafer with no peripheral transistors, hybrid-bond a matched low-voltage logic wafer carrying sense amps to its bitline face and a thick-oxide wafer carrying 3 V wordline drivers to its wordline face, each at ~0.5-1 um pitch.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7) and voltage floor (fact 10): each function gets its ideal process, the array wafer drops its periphery masks, and array efficiency rises toward ~90%, with periphery built on depreciated logic lines.

title: Threshold-coded tier select replaces the staircase
idea: Worse: carve a giant staircase so every tier gets its own contact, with area and trim steps growing linearly with tier count. Flip: dope each tier's built-in select transistor to one of several thresholds during in-situ deposition and drive a few shared vertical select gates with a voltage code that turns on exactly one tier, i.e., a binary decoder embedded in the stack.
why: Tier contacts drop from N to ~2*log2(N) lines; saves ~5-10% die area and dozens of trim/etch steps at 64+ tiers (facts 2, 7).

title: Workfunction charge-plasma junctions for implant-free stacked lateral transistors
idea: Charge-plasma effect: source and drain regions of the lateral access transistors in each deposited channel tier are induced electrostatically by low- and high-workfunction metal contacts, not by dopant implants. No implant has to pass through upper tiers, and no activation anneal is needed.
why: Unblocks the lateral transistor in 3D DRAM (fact 2) and keeps the thermal budget low; claim each tier is processed identically with no implant masks, so mask count does not grow with tier count.

title: NEMS relay logic failure repurposed: relays isolate dead tiers
idea: Nano-electro-mechanical (NEMS) relay logic has not been adopted because contacts stick after billions of cycles. A spare-tier switch needs only a few dozen actuations, so put NEMS relays on each tier's power and signal rails. A shorted or leaky tier is physically disconnected, with zero leakage, and a spare tier switched in.
why: Keeps one bad tier from killing a 26+ tier 3D DRAM stack (fact 2 yield) or an HBM stack (fact 6), with repair in the field.

title: Stacked CFET four-transistor loadless latch near DRAM footprint
idea: [Box: bistable latch | complementary stacked FET (nFET over pFET) | differential SA | monolithic CFET | Si | Si/SiGe epitaxy] Build a 4T loadless cell (two pMOS access devices plus two cross-coupled nMOS held by leakage ratio) with CFET vertical stacking so the footprint approaches ~2x a 6F2 DRAM cell, with no capacitor and no refresh.
why: Refresh (fact 3), capacitor (fact 1) and destructive read (fact 8): static, non-destructive cell on a logic process; trades ~2x area for no capacitor module.

title: Loadless leakage-ratio latch stacked in oxide TFT tiers
idea: Po: the leak holds the bit instead of stealing it. Stack a 4-transistor loadless latch (n-type oxide drivers, p-type SnO or Te access-loads) in two monolithic tiers sized so p-load off-current exceeds n-driver off-current >10x; leakage itself pulls each node toward its stored state, so the cell is static and needs no refresh.
why: Refresh eliminated with ~10 aW standby per cell; two-tier stacking gives ~8-10F2 footprint, far denser than planar 6T SRAM, and fits BEOL above logic.

title: Core-shell BaTiO3-alumina ink: printed high-k with leakage-blocking shells
idea: Formulate an ink of ~30 nm BaTiO3 nanoparticles each wrapped in a 2 nm Al2O3 shell, then print and compact a 60 nm dielectric, so high-k cores raise capacitance while continuous shells block grain-boundary leakage paths.
why: C=eA/d: a composite k of ~40-60 approaches the k~70 called for in fact 1 with a printable, low-temperature dielectric, letting foil cells shrink ~5x in area at equal charge.

title: Capacitor walls instead of pillars: line gratings segmented by self-aligned cuts
idea: [Box: MIM on both wall faces | VCT | charge-share SA | monolithic | Si | ArF SADP line gratings + cuts self-aligned to wordlines] Form storage electrodes as continuous tall oxide-core walls, far stiffer than isolated pillars so AR 120+ does not lean, coat both faces, then segment each wall into per-cell plates with cuts self-aligned to the wordlines.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1, AR ~115 target): line/space patterns suit ArF, and the extra height delivers more charge without EUV.

title: Capacitor wafer bonded beneath transistor wafer at cell pitch
idea: Po: the capacitor lives in another factory. Etch ultra-deep trench capacitors (AR 100-150 in single-crystal Si, which does not lean like stacked pillars) on a cheap mature-node 'capacitor wafer', layer-transfer a thin single-crystal Si film on top at <400 C, then build access transistors with laser anneal and self-aligned contacts down to each buried capacitor.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): ~2x Cs from deeper single-crystal trenches; decouples capacitor and transistor thermal budgets and moves the capacitor module to an older, cheaper fab (capital, fact 4).

title: Nanosheet-seeded glass grows high-k oriented perovskite capacitors
idea: IFR: 'k is so high the capacitor can be flat.' Backward: coat alkali-free glass with a Langmuir-Blodgett monolayer of Ca2Nb3O10 nanosheets that template (001)-oriented SrTiO3 or (Ba,Sr)TiO3 growth at <=600 C, giving k~200-300 films that a silicon BEOL cannot host, then stack oxide TFT cells over planar or shallow-trench capacitors.
why: Charge wall (fact 1 needs k~70): ~3-4x that target, so 5 fF fits in a <=10:1 structure and the 60-75:1 etch disappears.

title: Rutile TiO2 grown on the ruthenium bitline template
idea: Under 400 C, the Ru electrode lines of each tier are surface-oxidized to RuO2, which templates rutile Al-doped TiO2 by ALD at 280 C with k of about 80-100. These are planar or shallow-trench capacitors integrated straight onto the electrode tier.
why: Fact 1: reaches the k of about 70 the brief says is needed, so 5 fF fits at about 25:1 AR instead of 75:1.

title: Micro-transfer-printed silicon sense amplifiers dot a printed array foil
idea: Make 50x50 um sense-amp and decoder chiplets on a depreciated logic line, release them by undercut etch, and pick-and-print thousands per elastomer-stamp cycle onto the foil, one chiplet per ~1k x 1k printed sub-array.
why: Puts the speed- and matching-critical periphery (49%, fact 7) in silicon while the array stays at R2R cost; since transistor matching sets sense margin, silicon sense amps let printed cells hold less charge and reach ~10-30 ns access.

title: Self-ordered anodic alumina grows the capacitor mold
idea: Reverse etching a mold into growing one: deposit ~2 um of aluminum over the landing pads, use one added mask to imprint pore nucleation dimples aligned to the pads, and anodize so self-ordered pores grow straight down at AR >100; line the pores with TiN/high-k/TiN.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): AR 100-150 with no plasma HAR etch and no support-lattice masks; AAO pore AR >1000 is proven at larger pitch.

title: Taper-aware tiers: size each tier's cells to match the hole taper
idea: Accept the 88-89 degree taper of 1990s RIE instead of buying new tools, and design for the depth variation tier by tier: deeper tiers get thicker deposited gate layers, so a narrower hole at depth still yields matched transistor drive and capacitance.
why: High-AR etch is a 3D blocker (fact 2): a tool limit becomes a design parameter, letting old etchers handle 32+ tiers.

title: Eliminate the 12-die HBM stack: one monolithic 3D-tiered die
idea: Replace 12 thinned DRAM dies bonded with TSVs by one die with 48-96 monolithic array tiers over periphery, so there is a single grind, no TSV reveal CMP and no 11 repeated bond-surface preparations.
why: Water and HBM tax: backgrinding, TSV reveal CMP, bond prep cleans and dicing are repeated per die today; one die removes >90% of them and the TSV area tax.

title: Stomatal back-gate planes seal every 3D tier when idle
idea: Give each tier of a lateral-transistor 3D DRAM a buried conductive back-gate plane under its channel layer, driven strongly negative when that tier's banks are idle and relaxed during access, like stomata closing at night, using the plane's large capacitance as a slow low-power control.
why: Leakage tail and refresh: deep back-bias trims the off-current tail 10-100x in idle tiers, stretching refresh 10x+ and cutting refresh's 16-33% share of idle power.

title: Gain-cell NAND string with dual-gate bypassable read transistors
idea: [Box: storage-node gate | dual-gate IGZO 2T0C | series-string current sense | monolithic vertical string | Si | 3D-NAND hole-and-plate deposition] Build 2T0C gain cells along a vertical macaroni string like 3D NAND; each read transistor has a back word-plate that, driven high, forces it on regardless of its stored node, so unselected cells act as pass gates and only the selected cell's storage node modulates string current. Write transistors hang off a second vertical write-bitline in the same hole.
why: Attacks 'no manufacturable 3D cell' (fact 2) and the capacitor wall (fact 1): no capacitor at all, reuses 3D-NAND tier economics; 64-128 cells per hole could give ~5x bits per footprint vs 6F2 at F=12 nm.

title: Murray's-law tapered vascular power grids cut tungsten in tall stacks
idea: Size the vertical and lateral power and wordline-strap trees of a 3D DRAM like blood vessels obeying Murray's law (parent r^3 = sum of child r^3), with thick Cu 'arteries' tapering to thin Mo/Ru 'capillaries' only at cell level, instead of uniform tungsten straps everywhere.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) and IR drop in 100+ tier stacks: minimum metal volume for a given resistance; ~30-50% less refractory metal and lower IR drop.

title: Stepwise adiabatic bitline restore using spare-tier capacitors as reservoirs
idea: Dedicate a few cell rows per tier as reservoir capacitors held at V/4, V/2 and 3V/4; during restore and refresh, bitlines step through these reservoirs before the final rail connection, and falling bitlines replenish them.
why: Charging a capacitor in N equal steps dissipates CV^2/(2N) instead of CV^2/2, so four steps cut bitline restore loss ~4x; with refresh at ~46 fJ/bit (fact 3) and restore dominating activation energy (fact 8), this is a direct cut using cells already in the stack.

title: Glass-panel memory sheets on idle display fab lines
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: replace precious 300 mm wafers with cheap Gen-8.5 glass (~5.5 m2) and run 4-8 stacked layers of IGZO 2T0C gain cells at ~1.5 um rules on existing LCD/OLED backplane lines. Panels (~15-20 GB per layer) are diced into memory tiles for a CXL-attached 100-200 ns capacity tier.
why: Capital intensity and cost per bit: reuses depreciated display fabs (no EUV, no quartz crucibles, no Si wafers); target ~$2-5/GB with layer stacking vs ~4x-inflated DRAM contract prices.

title: Mask-free interference lithography for perfectly periodic cell arrays
idea: [Box: 1T1C | VCT | standard SA | monolithic | Si | 193 nm two/three-beam immersion interference + one spacer step + low-res block mask] DRAM arrays are periodic, so expose them with mask-less two- and three-beam 193 nm immersion interference (~34 nm half-pitch per shot, ~17 nm after one spacer step) and trim array edges with a cheap low-resolution DUV block mask.
why: No EUV (fact 4): no reticle and much simpler optics; litho cost per array layer could drop to roughly a fifth of EUV.

title: Ultra-wide-bandgap gallium-oxide vertical channels through every tier
idea: Po: the transistor is an insulator that occasionally conducts. Use ALD Ga2O3 (Eg ~4.8 eV, no hole conduction so no GIDL path) as a junctionless, fully depleted vertical access channel through each 3D tier; thermal generation scales as exp(-Eg/2kT), pushing off-current orders of magnitude below oxide channels like IGZO.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): <1e-20 A off-current gives hours of retention with ~2 fF at 85 C, so refresh never runs.

title: Calcium fluoride and silicon epitaxial superlattice yields insulated crystalline tiers
idea: Exploit CaF2's 0.6% lattice match to Si to grow Si/CaF2 epitaxial superlattices by MBE or low-temperature CVD, so every Si layer is a single-crystal device tier and every CaF2 layer (12 eV gap) is a built-in insulator that can also be recessed selectively to open capacitor cavities.
why: One-pass growth of crystalline SOI-like tiers with no bonding and no germanium (fact 2), from abundant Ca and F; CaF2 doubles as isolation and sacrificial layer.

title: 1310 nm optical links shine vertically through stacked silicon dies
idea: Exploit silicon's transparency beyond 1.1 um: each die carries micro-emitters and Ge photodiodes aligned through the stack, so data passes vertically as light through undrilled silicon, replacing signal TSVs and their keep-out zones.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): no drilled vias means no TSV area, no keep-out, no Cu-pumping yield loss and thicker, sturdier dies; the photon-energy floor (~1 eV per detected photon) leaves headroom for ~100 fJ/bit links.

title: Bismuth-tin capillary injection fills through-tier vias at 150 C
idea: As the final back-end step, evacuate the wafer, flood it with molten Bi58Sn42 (melts at 139 C) and apply gas pressure so liquid metal is forced into 50:1 through-tier vias and staircase contacts in seconds; wipe and polish the excess for void-free vertical connections.
why: Removes tungsten and slow CVD fills from deep contacts (resource and capital) at a temperature compatible with oxide-TFT tiers; a vacuum chamber and hotplate suffice in a university lab.

title: Fresnel capacitor: nested shallow shells replace one tall pillar
idea: As a Fresnel lens collapses a thick lens into concentric rings, collapse a 75:1 pillar into 3-4 concentric electrode shells nested in one cell footprint: alternate ALD of TiN, high-k and a sacrificial spacer inside a single ~20:1 hole, then selectively strip the spacers so both faces of every shell become capacitor area.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): roughly the area of a 75:1 pillar at AR ~20, cutting the hardest etch depth 3-4x and pillar leaning; claims 5 fF at a fraction of the high-AR etch cost.

title: Identical tiers self-number at power-up for stack-to-order capacity
idea: Po: tiers don't know who they are. Design every tier from one mask set with no tier-specific wiring; a daisy-chained token climbs the stack at power-up and each tier latches its address, so one assembly line builds 4- to 64-tier parts from the same wafers to match weekly demand.
why: Masks and capital: one mask set instead of per-tier variants; build-to-order capacity raises usable supply during shortages.

title: DUV photo-annealed printed oxide memory tiers atop finished logic dies
idea: Nanoimprint and inkjet-print metal-oxide TFT DRAM tiers directly on a finished logic wafer's passivation, converting sol-gel films with 185/254 nm UV below 150 C so the 400 C back-end budget is never approached, in an advanced-packaging house.
why: Data movement (fact 5): memory sits micrometres above the compute it feeds, so wire energy for the hot working set falls ~10-30x versus HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit, without hybrid bonding or a DRAM fab.

title: Magnify contributors: open-source 3D DRAM compiler and PDK
idea: Fund three engineers to release an open-source array generator for SKY130 and GF180, plus a parametric 3D DRAM tier model (tier count, Cs, leakage tail, spares) and a cost and yield calculator, so universities can tape out DRAM arrays on open shuttles.
why: U.S. manufacturability and talent: brings hundreds of designers to array architecture for about $900k.

title: Twistor helical-anisotropy nanowires that write and sense through every tier
idea: Revive Bell's twistor (magnetic tape wound helically on a wire): grow vertical nanowires whose magnetic shell has a helical easy axis set by a twisted strain field, so an axial bitline current plus one tier strap's field switches only the crossing, and readout uses the inverse-Wiedemann voltage pulse induced along the same wire.
why: Facts 2 and 7: transistor-free vertical array where each pillar is both write and sense line for all tiers; per-cell device count and periphery drop sharply if the twist works below 50 nm.

title: RAID across tiers: one parity tier per sixteen
idea: Worse: let one defective tier among 200 kill or degrade the die. Flip: write each 16-tier group with an XOR parity tier computed in the base die and reconstruct a failed tier's bits on read, so random tier defects become correctable instead of becoming yield loss.
why: At 200 tiers, tier-defect yield^N would wreck cost per good bit; ~6% parity overhead holds die yield near 2D levels, so 10x density survives at the same cost (facts 2, 6).

title: Ge-fraction-coded superlattice: chemistry, not overlay, cuts every cell part
idea: Worse: align each tier's transistor, gate and capacitor regions with separate masks whose overlay drifts tier by tier. Flip: grow all tiers in one epitaxy run with sublayers of different Ge fraction, then from a single vertical slit run composition-selective lateral etches whose recess depth scales with Ge content, so capacitor cavity, gate recess and spacer of every tier are cut in a few etches, self-aligned by chemistry.
why: Per-tier masks and overlay error go to zero (facts 2, 4), so added tiers cost only epitaxy time.

title: Parametron phase bits held by pumped NEMS beams in stacked cavities
idea: Revive Goto's parametron: each cell is a nanomechanical beam parametrically pumped at 2f by a tier-wide electrostatic line, ringing at f with phase 0 or pi and holding that bit as long as the pump runs. Tiers of vacuum-sealed beams stack in BEOL, and reads use phase-sensitive capacitive pickup on the bitline.
why: Facts 1 and 3: no capacitor charge wall and no refresh; hold power is set by beam Q (~1e4) through one shared pump rather than 46 fJ/bit refresh.

title: All-epitaxial Si/SiGe stack etched only with HBr/Cl2 chemistry
idea: Substitute the oxide/nitride stack of 3D DRAM (etched with C4F6/C4F8/CH2F2) with an all-semiconductor Si/SiGe epitaxial stack whose slits and holes are etched only with HBr/Cl2/O2 at cryogenic chuck temperature (SiOxBry sidewall passivation), deferring every dielectric to non-fluorinated fills (aminosilane ALD SiO2, TMA Al2O3) planarized by CMP instead of etch-back.
why: Builds the 26-100 tier stacks 3D DRAM needs (fact 2) without fluorocarbon gases (GWP up to ~9,000) or their abatement, keeping single-crystal channels for a tight leakage tail.

title: Convert idle 3D-NAND lines to vertical floating-body DRAM strings
idea: Worse: insist new DRAM capacity needs new $15B DRAM fabs. Flip: toll existing 200+-layer 3D NAND lines (same oxide/nitride stack, channel-hole etch, staircase) to build vertical-channel capacitorless floating-body cells by swapping the charge-trap film for a thin gate oxide and adding a hole-reservoir body contact, then sell DRAM-class strings under take-or-pay tolling contracts.
why: At NAND-class wafer cost, 200 tiers at 1 bit/cell gives ~5-7 Gb/mm2 versus ~0.5 Gb/mm2 for 2D DRAM (>10x) and reuses tools already paid for (fact 4: 3-5 years, $15B); floating-body retention and refresh load are the main risk.

title: Coarse-litho tall stack: 48 ArF-dry tiers beat EUV density
idea: Because nothing exceeds 400 C, oxide 4F2 cross-point tiers can be stacked sequentially without disturbing lower tiers. Each tier uses only two ArF-dry masks at 65 nm, and density comes from tier count instead of litho.
why: Fact 4: 48 tiers at 65 nm 4F2 give about 350 nm2/bit (2.5x denser than 6F2 at 12 nm) with zero EUV; capital moves to cheap litho.

title: Pin-art toy: alignment-free bonding onto an unpatterned nano-capacitor forest
idea: Like a pin-art toy taking any shape, make a separate capacitor wafer as an unpatterned forest of isolated 8 nm-pitch nanopillar capacitors (separate bottom electrodes, common top plate), then hybrid-bond it to the transistor wafer. Each ~20 nm landing pad touches 4-6 pillars in parallel while pillars over the gaps touch nothing, so the capacitor needs no mask and zero overlay to the cells.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and litho capital (fact 4): the critical capacitor-hole EUV layer disappears and capacitors come from a cheap separate fab; claim -1 to -2 EUV layers and ~10% lower wafer cost.

title: Rolling probe-wheel test and laser-fuse repair inline on the web
idea: Run each printed array web under a roller probe that contacts test pads at line speed, measure every mat's retention and margin, and immediately laser-cut printed fuses to remap failing mats to ~3% spares before lamination.
why: Poisson yield Y=exp(-D*A) with printed defect densities of ~10/cm^2 still gives ~99% for 0.001 cm^2 mats, so cheap spares rather than cleanroom class set yield, keeping cost per bit near the raw R2R area cost.

title: Carbon-chain block copolymers self-assemble the 4F2 cell grid without EUV
idea: Spin cylinder-forming PS-b-PMMA (or high-chi PS-b-PDMS) on a coarse e-beam/i-line guide pattern so it self-assembles a hexagonal hole array at 20-24 nm pitch, remove the minority cores, and transfer the holes into an Al2O3 hard mask for vertical-channel 4F2 pillars.
why: Replaces 2-3 EUV layers (fact 4) with a polymer coat and hotplate while reaching 4F2 density (1.5x vs 6F2); needs only a spinner, oven and RIE found in any university fab.

title: Plywood memory: laminate 64 pre-tested thin-film array foils
idea: Scale up to the plywood mill: build thin-film array layers on 4-um polyimide over glass carriers at 180-nm rules and test each foil. Laminate known-good foils face-to-face with anisotropic conductive film, whose ~1-um particles form the inter-foil vias, and stack 64 layers.
why: Tier yield and capital (facts 2, 4): stacking only known-good layers avoids compound yield loss, on 1990s-class tools.

title: Eliminate the zero-defect assumption: defect-tolerant arrays allow fewer rinses
idea: Design mats with fine-grained remapping and per-mat ECC so random particle and metal defects cost capacity rather than dies, then run the fab with far fewer UPW rinse cycles and recycled rinse water, trading 1-3% capacity for yield-insensitive processing.
why: Water: ultrapure rinse volume is set by yield sensitivity to contamination; a defect-absorbing architecture lets the fab cut rinse volume ~10x, though metal contamination raising the leakage tail is the main risk.

title: Water-droplet self-alignment with alkylsilane rings replaces precision die placement
idea: Substitute high-precision pick-and-place for die-to-wafer DRAM stacking with capillary self-alignment: a water droplet on each hydrophilic bond site pulls the coarsely dropped die into ~0.2 um registration, the surrounding hydrophobic ring made from octadecyltrichlorosilane or plasma-polymerized HMDSO instead of the usual fluorinated FDTS.
why: Stacking capital and throughput (fact 6): parallel, tool-light alignment for thousands of dies per minute, enabling finer hybrid-bond pitch per dollar.

title: Elevator counterweight: two tiers in series voltage domains recycle charge
idea: A counterweight falls as the car rises: run two cell tiers (or two stacked dies) in series voltage domains, the lower array between ground and mid-rail and the upper between mid-rail and supply, so the charge one tier dumps during precharge and restore becomes the supply charge of the other. A small on-die balancing regulator absorbs mismatch, and external rails and the interface stay standard.
why: Voltage floor and CV2 energy (fact 10): array charge drawn from the supply roughly halves, about -40% array activation energy.

title: Per-tier 2T preamp at pillar junction cuts needed charge 5x
idea: Inverts 'bitlines are passive wires to an edge sense amp.' Place a two-transistor gain stage where each tier's short local bitline meets the vertical global bitline, so the storage node drives a gate instead of a long line, letting Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~1 fF.
why: Fact 1: capacitor height/AR can drop ~5x, turning 3D capacitors into flat lateral plates.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM bonded under a wafer-scale accelerator replaces HBM
idea: Substitute HBM stacks plus interposer with one full DRAM wafer hybrid-bonded face-to-face to a wafer-scale processor: each compute tile gets the DRAM directly beneath it through ~2 um-pitch bonds, and defective DRAM tiles are routed around by the processor's existing redundancy fabric.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~3-4 pJ/bit -> <0.3 pJ/bit and >10x bandwidth per mm², with no TSVs (fact 6) and no reticle-limited interposer.

title: Monolayer MoS2 tiers at 15 nm pitch: 256 tiers per 4 um
idea: Under 400 C, wafer-scale MOCVD grows monolayer MoS2 (0.7 nm channel) for each tier. With an ALD gate stack, each tier is about 15 nm thick, and the atomic-thin body plus 1.8 eV gap gives aA-level leakage.
why: Facts 2 and 3: about 3x more tiers per stack height than Si tiers (about 45 nm), and refresh intervals stretch from 64 ms toward minutes.

title: Resin-vat recoating: spin-on liquid oxide tiers cured by UV
idea: SLA 3D printers recoat liquid resin and cure layer by layer; stack tiers by spin-coating solution In-Zn-O semiconductor and spin-on high-k, curing each with deep-UV photochemical activation below 250 C on existing coat/track tools, patterned with KrF masks.
why: Vacuum-free tier deposition slashes per-tier capex and lets old track tools add oxide gain-cell tiers on logic BEOL (facts 2, 4), avoiding new ALD and sputter capacity.

title: Dealloyed nanoporous TiN sponge replaces smooth capacitor electrodes
idea: Substitute the smooth storage-node TiN with a nanoporous one: ALD a TiN/AlN nanolaminate electrode (TiCl4/TMA/NH3), selectively leach the Al phase in dilute NaOH/TMAH to leave a 3D sponge with 5-10 nm ligaments, then conformally coat with ALD ZrO2 and top TiN.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): 2-3x electrode area in the same pillar (Cs 5 -> 10+ fF) without raising AR; no HF needed.

title: Ballroom mirror twins: one self-mating die forms a two-high stack
idea: Two identical dancers form a pair by mirroring. Design one die whose bond-face pad map is 180-degree symmetric, then wafer-to-wafer bond two identical wafers, one rotated. A mode fuse makes one die's periphery serve both arrays and power-gates the twin's.
why: A 2-high F2F memory stack from a single mask set and wafer type halves mask NRE. The bonding service is buyable by a small team (capital, Fact 7).

title: Plate-tier capacitor: storage node overlaps an interleaved plate layer
idea: IFR: 'the capacitor takes no extra area or height.' Backward: alternate every channel tier with a thin plate-electrode tier separated by 4-6 nm high-k, so each lateral cell's storage node is a parallel-plate capacitor over its own top and bottom footprint (~0.25 fF at k=40), with no lateral capacitor arm; pair with short local bitlines that need only that much charge.
why: 3D blocker (fact 2): removes the lateral capacitor, shortening the cell ~2-3x and lowering the ~26-tier break-even toward ~12 tiers.

title: Dealloyed nanoporous electrode multiplies capacitor area without height
idea: IFR: 'the capacitor has infinite area in a tiny height.' Backward: deposit the bottom electrode as an alloy (e.g., Ni-Al or Cu-Mn), selectively dissolve the sacrificial metal to leave a 3-5 nm ligament nanoporous sponge, then ALD high-k and a conformal top electrode, giving 4-8x the surface of a smooth pillar.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): 5 fF at ~15-20:1 aspect ratio instead of 60-75:1, cutting the hardest etch and pillar-collapse yield loss.

title: Photonic HBM base die from a US silicon-photonics foundry
idea: Merge the HBM logic base die with optical transceivers built at a US photonics fab (e.g., GF Fotonix, Malta NY): DRAM cores stack on a base die that speaks WDM over fiber, so the stack needs no 2.5D interposer beside the GPU and can sit centimeters to meters away.
why: Removes dependence on offshore CoWoS interposers and frees placement for more stacks per accelerator; ~1-2 pJ/bit links versus 3-4 pJ/bit HBM (fact 5).

title: ISO shipping-container standard for interchangeable memory tiers
idea: Like the ISO container standard, publish an open 'memory brick' spec: fixed 1 um hybrid-bond grid, power/signal pin map, test hooks and thickness, so any vendor's array tier or logic base stacks with any other.
why: Breaks HBM's vertically integrated stack (fact 6), lets U.S. fabs make bases or tiers separately, and pools capacity across many fabs; stack NRE down ~50%.

title: Used-ship market: depreciated 200 mm fabs build deep tier stacks
idea: Like shipping firms buying used vessels, acquire fully depreciated 65-180 nm 200 mm fabs and run only deposition-heavy 256-tier vertical stacks at ~90 nm pitch (one KrF/i-line litho per 64 tiers), bonding a thin modern logic base later.
why: Depreciation (~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) goes to ~zero while 256 tiers at 90 nm still give ~8 Gb/mm2; ~30-100x lower cost per bit; trade-offs: big die, ~200 ns latency.

title: Magnify effective capacity: compression engine in the base die
idea: Prototype a stack whose logic base die compresses cache lines inline, with 64B lines packed into variable slots by a metadata table, using an FPGA in front of commodity DRAM. Then tape out the engine as a $200k chiplet.
why: Supply: about 1.5-2x effective capacity on compressible AI and server data from the same DRAM bits.

title: Swiss-cheese tiers: stack defective layers, remap holes in base die
idea: Inverts 'every cell in a die must work.' Accept 3D tiers with up to ~5-10% dead cells, map defects at wafer probe into a per-stack CAM/remap table held in the logic base die, and drop per-tier redundancy rows/columns, so tier yields no longer multiply into stack yield.
why: Fact 2: lowers the yield-driven break-even tier count (26+) and recovers ~3-5% redundancy area; makes 100-tier stacks economically yieldable.

title: Millimeter mat-lets fluidically self-assembled onto logic base wafers
idea: Dice DRAM arrays into ~1 mm^2 tested mat-lets and flow them in a carrier fluid over a logic wafer with shape-matched recesses, where they self-align and solder at millions per hour, so only known-good mats enter a stack or 2.5D tile.
why: Yield follows Y=exp(-D*A): at D=0.1/cm^2, 1 mm^2 parts yield ~99.9% versus ~90% for 1 cm^2 dies, compounding across 12-16 die HBM stacks, so the 20-30% HBM yield loss (fact 6) falls to a few percent.

title: Bookshelf: dies stand on edge, bonded spine-down onto logic
idea: Books stand spine-out on a shelf: dice 30 um DRAM dies, polish one edge to expose bitline and I/O wires routed there, then stand 100+ dies upright and hybrid-bond their edges onto a logic base die. Each edge carries thousands of wires at ~2 um pitch, and no die needs a TSV.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and data movement (fact 5): no TSV area or yield loss, one base die hosts 100+ dies with short uniform wires; claim ~1 pJ/bit and TB-class stacks.

title: Dies stand edge-on on the base die, wired through cut edges
idea: [Box: standard 1T1C | Si FET | conventional SA | edge-mounted 'bookshelf' dies | thinned Si | dicing exposes top metal + edge micro-bump plating] Instead of stacking DRAM dies flat with TSVs, stand thinned dies vertically on the logic base die and bring thousands of fine wires out of the polished die edge, where top-metal lines exposed by dicing are plated into edge bumps.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out area and no thinning/TSV yield loss (20-30%); capacity scales with dies per row rather than stack height.

title: Monolithic stack whose vertical bitlines replace HBM's TSV die stack
idea: Worse: build 12 separate DRAM dies, each losing area to TSV keep-out zones and microbumps, and stack them. Flip: fabricate one monolithic many-tier array whose vertical global bitlines run through the tiers as native interconnect, bonded once to a logic base die, so the 12-high TSV stack becomes one die and one bond.
why: Removes the ~3x area-per-bit HBM TSV tax and the 20-30% stack-yield loss (fact 6): one bond instead of twelve.

title: HMC logic base die made detachable with liquid-metal microbumps
idea: HMC died partly because its logic base die tied the DRAM stack to one controller generation. Join the base die to the DRAM core stack with gallium-indium liquid-metal microbumps held in polymer cups. Warming slightly releases the joint, so a stack can move to a new base die (for example a new CXL/UCIe PHY) and a failed base die can be replaced.
why: DRAM core dies outlive 2-3 controller generations, about doubling the useful life of scarce bits, and repair needs no stack scrap (fact 6).

title: Nitrogen-rich strained SiN bilayers roll planar arrays into memory scrolls
idea: Build a planar oxide-TFT DRAM array with i-line litho on a stress-graded SiNx bilayer over a sacrificial layer; releasing it makes the membrane self-roll into a 10-20-winding Swiss roll, turning the 2D array into a 3D cylinder with ~15 effective tiers per footprint, wired out through the unrolled tail.
why: Gets 3D layer count from 2D lithography with zero high-aspect etching (facts 2, 4); rolled-up nanomembranes are an established university technique, so a prototype memory scroll is buildable now.

title: Plywood memory: laminate 100 printed DRAM foils with edge microvias
idea: Test each 25 um printed DRAM foil, laminate 100 known-good foils with B-stage adhesive, then UV-laser drill and silver-paste fill vias through a peripheral via field to a shared bus, with each foil carrying a printed tier-select switch.
why: 3D integration without a fab: each added layer costs a lamination, not a deposition cycle, so a 10x10 cm, 2.5 mm block holds ~60 GB, and layer count passes the 26-tier break-even (fact 2) with zero EUV (fact 4).

title: Passing-gate trenches become shield lines that back-bias neighbors
idea: Combine row-hammer shielding and leakage control in one buried trench: every passing-gate buried wordline is replaced by a line held at about -0.5 V that both screens active rows from aggressor coupling and back-gates the adjacent access channels into deeper off-state.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and leakage tail (fact 3): removes the passing-gate hammer path (threshold up >10x) and cuts GIDL/subthreshold tail ~10x for ~4-8x longer refresh; area cost offset by deleting hammer-tracking logic.

title: Argon-activated room-temperature bonding stacks finished oxide-TFT memory tiers
idea: Fabricate oxide-semiconductor memory tiers on separate 100 mm wafers, activate both bonding faces with an Ar fast-atom beam or Ar plasma, bond in vacuum at room temperature, then grind/etch away the donor substrate; repeat for 4-8 tiers on IR-aligned keys.
why: Stacks fully processed tiers with zero thermal budget so each is optimized independently (fact 2) and tests a known-good-tier yield model; argon is abundant (0.93% of air) and SAB bonders exist in many universities.

title: Socketed DRAM chips return as MEMS micro-spring die sockets
idea: Socketed DIP DRAM was abandoned because of contact reliability and size. Use lithographically defined MEMS micro-springs, as in probe cards, as a permanent fine-pitch die socket on the interposer. A lid holds the HBM stack down, and it can be lifted out, retested and replaced.
why: Fixes HBM's irreparability and yield scrap (fact 6). Good stacks and interposers are reused instead of scrapped with the assembly.

title: Core-memory coincident-current selection with dual-gate 3D cells, no tier decoders
idea: Revive core memory's X/Y coincident-current selection: each 3D cell's access device is a dual-gate thin-film transistor that conducts only when both its tier strap and its vertical pillar gate are at half-select level, so N tier straps plus M pillars address N x M cells with only N+M drivers. Half-selected cells see one gate on and stay off, exactly as half-selected cores stayed below coercive force.
why: Facts 2 and 7: removes per-tier word drivers and most staircase decode, cutting periphery from ~49% toward ~30% and lowering the tier count needed to break even below 26.

title: Gain-cell shadow-row tier replaces the sense-amp latch as row buffer
idea: Substitute the single sense-amp row buffer per bank with an extra top tier of nondestructive 3T oxide-semiconductor gain cells over each sub-array holding 8-16 'shadow rows'; an activated row is copied once into a shadow, and later hits and re-opens read the shadow without re-activating or re-restoring the DRAM row.
why: Destructive read (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): est. 3-5x fewer activations on server traces, cutting ACT energy and aggressor counts; the tier is stacked, not added to footprint (~5% cost).

title: Advance market commitment paying only for 10x-density, cost-parity DRAM
idea: Worse: subsidize fab floor space that just replicates 6F2 DRAM. Flip: a U.S. government plus hyperscaler buyers' club pre-commits to buy a fixed volume (e.g., 10 EB) at today's $/wafer-equivalent only from parts with >=10x bits/mm2 versus 1-gamma DRAM, paying milestone premiums for tier-yield results and nothing for raw capacity.
why: A pull incentive aimed exactly at the 10x-density, same-cost target that de-risks the 3-5 year, $15B bet (fact 4) for whichever 3D architecture wins, and anchors the output in U.S. fabs.

title: Edinburgh-rock fiber draw: slice prebuilt vertical cell arrays from preforms
idea: Borrow optical-fiber drawing and seaside rock-candy making: assemble a macroscopic preform of doped-Si-core rods clad in gate glass, metal-glass gate sleeves and capacitor shells, co-draw it ~1000x, bundle and redraw to ~40 nm cell pitch, then wafer-slice the boule crosswise so every slice is a ready-made 4F2 vertical-transistor array needing only top and bottom wiring.
why: Litho-bound scaling and capital (fact 4): array pitch is set by draw ratio, not EUV, and one draw-tower run yields thousands of slices; claimed 5-10x lower array capex. Molten-core Si fiber draw exists, but device-grade co-drawn junctions are unproven.

title: Child's LEGO staircase: shingled die stack with printed edge wires
idea: A child stacks bricks in a staircase. Shingle-stack 16 thinned DRAM dies with an offset, then aerosol-jet print silver-nanoparticle traces down the stair edges to connect the stack. The tools are a ~$1M printer and die bonder a 10-person team can run.
why: Removes TSV keep-out area and the 20-30% HBM yield loss (Fact 6) for a mid-bandwidth stack of ~500 IO from two staircase edges.

title: Short wordline segments with bonded local drivers make resistive TiN fine
idea: Inverts 'wordlines need a low-resistivity metal.' Cut every wordline into 32-64-cell segments, each fed by its own driver in the hybrid-bonded logic wafer below, so plain TiN or degenerately doped Si wordlines meet RC targets without W, Co or Ru.
why: Scarce resources and fact 10: removes chokepoint metals by architecture; shorter lines also cut wordline CV² energy ~2-4x.

title: Giant-display lesson: blue diode lasers crystallize silicon for stacked tiers
idea: Gen-10 display fabs crystallize silicon over square meters with XeCl excimer lasers that consume xenon and neon; replace them with line-scanned 450 nm GaN diode-laser arrays to melt-crystallize thin amorphous silicon (PECVD in SiH4/H2) on top of each finished DRAM tier. The heat stays in ~100 nm, so lower tiers stay below 400 C while the new tier gets large-grain channels for its access transistors.
why: Monolithic tier stacking (fact 2) without a bond per tier and without xenon or neon; ~200 cm2/Vs channels for 3D cells.

title: Electroformed copper-filament spare vias repair bonded stacks after test
idea: Ion migration (electrochemical metallization): every hybrid-bond interface carries a grid of spare Cu/SiO2 cells. After post-stack test, a forming voltage drives Cu ions into permanent filaments that reroute signals and power around failed bond pads or bad tiers, like antifuses in the third dimension.
why: Raises HBM and 3D stack yield, which loses 20-30% to bond defects (fact 6); claim recovers 10-20 yield points and so lowers cost per good bit.

title: Hot-aisle/cold-aisle tier zoning with embedded heat-spreader planes
idea: Scale datacenter airflow zoning down to a 3D die: insert a 50-nm AlN or diamond-like-carbon heat-spreader plane every 16 tiers, tie the planes to sidewall thermal vias, and put logic-heavy tiers at the hot end and cell tiers at the cold end. Leakage halves for every ~10 C, so a 20 C cooler cell tier needs a quarter of the refresh.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (fact 3) and the thermal wall of tall stacks: ~4x less refresh, and more tiers can sit over hot logic.

title: Minify the cost of discovery: an 8-tier DRAM inducement prize
idea: Put up a $400k prize, verified at a neutral university lab, for the first open demonstration of a stack of at least 8 tiers with at least 1 fF per cell and 64 ms retention. The winner grants the sponsor a licensing option.
why: 3D DRAM blocker: buys many parallel attempts for the price of one engineer team.

title: AI decode sweep doubles as free refresh by layout
idea: Po: the workload is the refresh controller. Stripe LLM weights so each token's matrix-vector pass activates every row of every bank and tier exactly once, guaranteeing a full sweep every 20-40 ms; row-open counters (already present for row-hammer tracking) certify coverage and the device issues zero refresh commands.
why: Refresh (fact 3): for inference memory, refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth tax drop to zero because activation already restores charge.

title: Back-plane under each tier becomes a retention lock
idea: Reverse the gate side: each IGZO tier sits on a blanket conductive back-plane, held at 0 V during access and pulsed to about -1 V when the subarray idles, pushing the channel deep into depletion. The only added mask is the back-plane contact.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): decades lower off-current during idle, potentially second-scale retention and near-zero refresh power in standby.

title: Tape-transferred monolayer MoS2 tiers, 20 nm per tier
idea: Inverts 'tiers must be grown on the wafer they live on.' Grow monolayer MoS2 access-transistor films on separate sapphire carriers by MOCVD and dry-transfer each 0.7 nm channel onto the stack, so 100 tiers fit in ~2 um and the ~1.8 eV gap suppresses the leakage tail.
why: Facts 2-3: thin tiers keep 100+ tier stacks etchable; the wider gap cuts the leakage tail by orders of magnitude and stretches refresh intervals.

title: Pre-outfitted tier blocks with local sense amps for digital stacking
idea: Shipyards fit pipes and wiring into hull blocks before joining them; likewise give every bonded array tier its own thin-film IGZO sense amplifiers and latches, so inter-tier bonds carry latched digital data at relaxed pitch instead of one analog bitline per bond.
why: Bond pitch can relax ~10x with digital links, raising hybrid-bond yield, and short tier-local bitlines cut CV2 energy; distributes the 49% periphery (fact 7) and trims data-movement energy (fact 5).

title: One wordline metal gates IGZO tiers above and below
idea: [Box: lateral 1T1C | top- and bottom-gated IGZO pair | standard SA | monolithic 3D | Si | ALD stack, ArF hole/slit patterning only] Order each repeat as IGZO / gate oxide / wordline / gate oxide / IGZO so a single wordline gates two cell layers, removing one metal layer per pair of tiers.
why: 3D tiers (fact 2): ~30% thinner stack per bit means shallower high-AR etches for the same bit count; density comes from deposition, not lithography.

title: One grayscale mask cuts every 3D tier contact
idea: Replace the multi-mask trim-etch staircase with a single grayscale reticle whose resist-thickness steps transfer through a proportional etch, opening contacts to all 64 tiers at graded depths in one exposure: a reversed staircase made of holes instead of terraces.
why: 3D cost (fact 2): staircase masks drop from ~4-8 to 1 and staircase area shrinks ~3x, moving break-even toward fewer tiers.

title: Rotate alternate mats 90 degrees for transposed access
idea: Rotate every second mat 90 degrees in layout (zero added masks), so data written row-major lands column-major there; the controller reads a matrix row from normal mats or its transpose from rotated mats with a single activation.
why: Data movement (fact 5): AI transposes (attention K^T, gradients) no longer move through caches, saving a read/write round trip of ~10-20 pJ/bit per transposed byte.

title: One hole, a hundred capacitors: tier-segmented storage rings
idea: Worse: etch a separate deep hole for every capacitor. Flip: in a lateral-transistor 3D stack, etch one vertical hole per cell column, recess each tier's channel end into a ring-shaped storage node, line the hole with one high-k film and fill it with a single common plate core, so every tier's capacitor is a segment of the same hole.
why: Capacitor etch, dielectric and plate are paid once for N tiers: 100 tiers at ~60F2 footprint per tier-cell gives ~86 nm2/bit (~10x) at deposition-dominated cost similar to today's wafer; the ~1 fF rings require short segmented bitlines (high risk).

title: Wedge-polished ramp exposes all tiers to one contact mask
idea: Worse: build the staircase with one resist-trim/etch cycle per tier pair so contact cost grows linearly with tiers. Flip: taper a narrow band at the array edge to a ~5 degree ramp with angled CMP or ion-beam polishing, exposing every tier as a ~0.5 um stripe on the slope, then land all tier contacts with a single DUV mask.
why: Staircase cost becomes O(1) instead of O(N), so scaling from 30 to 300 tiers (the 10x lever) adds deposition but no staircase steps or trim cycles (facts 2, 4, 7).

title: Bevel-lapped staircase: polish a shallow angle to expose every tier
idea: Use a 1960s bevel-and-stain trick as a scale magnifier: mechanically lap the tier stack's edge at ~0.5 degrees, which stretches each 50-nm tier into a ~6-um stripe on the surface, then contact every tier with a single 180-nm litho step.
why: A staircase needs litho and trim cycles for every tier (facts 2, 4): one polish and one mask replace N trims.

title: Interfacial phase-change superlattices on vertical-bitline hole sidewalls
idea: Interfacial phase change: an ALD-deposited GeTe/Sb2Te3 superlattice switches by flipping Ge atoms at the interfaces, not by melting, cutting energy ~10x. The superlattice lines the sidewalls of vertical bitline holes crossing horizontal wordline plates, making a VRRAM-style 3D array with a single-mask hole etch.
why: Gives dense non-volatile 3D cells (fact 2) with low capital (fact 4); claim tier count scales like 3D NAND, with 10x lower switching energy than PCM.

title: One nanoimprint template patterns all thirty-two identical tiers
idea: Under 400 C, room-temperature nanoimprint lithography patterns every oxide tier at 14 nm half-pitch with a single master template, because all tiers are identical. A self-aligned crossed-line imprint relaxes overlay.
why: Fact 4: tool capex about 1/4 of EUV, and template cost is spread over 32 tiers.

title: Transferred 2D-crystal tiers replace deposited semiconductor tiers
idea: Substitute epitaxial/deposited tier stacks with wafer-scale dry transfer of MOCVD monolayer MoS2 channels plus hBN gate dielectric grown on reusable sapphire donors, stacked tier by tier with a non-fluorinated polymer handle (PPC); each cell tier including its gate is <10 nm thick.
why: Tier pitch ~60+ nm (Si/SiGe) -> ~20-30 nm, 2-3x more tiers per um of stack and lower slit/hole AR (fact 2); 1.8 eV channel pushes leakage orders of magnitude below the 13 fA tail (fact 3).

title: Snack-bag web metallizers vacuum-coat 128-tier stacks by the kilometer
idea: Borrowed from roll-to-roll metallizers that coat packaging film at ~1,000 m/min: deposit 128 alternating Mo/SiOx wordline/insulator layers on a heat-tolerant web in multi-drum passes, laminate the stack onto a CMOS wafer, then one hole etch plus ALD finishes vertical-channel gain cells.
why: Tier-stack deposition is a dominant 3D cost; web coating is ~100x cheaper per m2, and with one mask for all tiers the path reaches ~$0.1/GB; trade-offs: lamination voids, lower tier quality, refresh-heavy cells.

title: Magnify the 3D array 20x to measure parasitics cheaply
idea: Build 3D tier stacks at 20x feature size with contact lithography but identical aspect ratios and materials, and measure their tier-to-tier and BL-BL coupling and RC directly. Calibrate 3D DRAM design models for about $150k.
why: Speeds up 3D array design: capacitive coupling scales geometrically, so a cheap magnified twin gives real parasitic data years before nm tiers exist.

title: Lift-slab tier manufacturing across idle mature fabs
idea: Like lift-slab construction where floors are cast on the ground and jacked into place, run each tier of a bonded 3D DRAM stack as a simple array-only wafer (1-2 critical layers) in under-used U.S. 65-28 nm fabs, then ship tier wafers to one bonding hub that hybrid-bonds and thins them into 8-16 tier stacks.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (fact 4, resources): reuses depreciated fabs instead of $15B greenfield; claims U.S. DRAM capacity without EUV at ~3-4x lower capex per wafer-tier.

title: Hydrogen backside gas replaces helium in cryo-etch of 3D stacks
idea: Inverts 'wafer chucks need helium backside cooling.' Use low-pressure H2 (higher thermal conductivity than He) as the backside heat-transfer gas for cryogenic high-aspect-ratio etch of 100+ tier stacks, with leak-tight chucks and point-of-use electrolytic H2.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar ~30% offline): keeps 3D-stack etch running with no He; cryo etch is what makes 100+ tiers etchable.

title: Hydrogen backside cooling for cryogenic high-aspect-ratio etch, helium-free
idea: Etch tools cool wafers with helium between wafer and chuck; hydrogen conducts heat slightly better than helium, so run cryogenic (-110 C) SF6/O2 etch of capacitor holes and tier stacks with low-pressure H2 backside gas, using liquid-hydrogen rocket practice for sensors and inerted lines. Cryo etch passivates sidewalls with SiOxFy and needs no argon, giving vertical profiles at high AR.
why: Removes helium from every etch chamber; AR 100+ cryo etch for capacitors (fact 1) and tier stacks (fact 2) with better chuck uniformity.

title: Deep-sea pressure: high-pressure deuterium anneal heals stacked-tier traps
idea: Deep-ocean hardware shows how pressure drives gas into solids; anneal finished 3D DRAM tier stacks in 20-50 atm deuterium/nitrogen at <=400 C so deuterium penetrates many tiers and passivates the channel and interface traps behind the leakage tail, staying within the stack's thermal budget. Deuterium bonds resist hot-carrier and activation-stress depassivation.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): tail traps cut ~2-5x, lengthening refresh; trap-assisted row hammer (fact 9) reduced; no argon or helium ambient.
